Christ appointed Paul; grace and peace come from God (verses 1–5)

Paul was appointed an apostle directly by Jesus Christ, and therefore also by God the Father, who shares the Son's divine nature and appointed him to be Mediator.

Grace includes both God's loving favor toward us and the good work he performs within us.

Peace includes the inward comfort and outward wellbeing that are truly necessary for us.

Both blessings flow from the Father as their source through Jesus Christ.

Notice the order: grace first, then peace. Genuine peace cannot exist without grace.

Christ gave himself for our sins to make atonement for us. God's justice required that sacrifice, and Jesus accepted it willingly.

Consider the infinite cost paid for our sins!

Sin is so destructive that nothing less than the gift of the Son of God could put it away.

We ought to understand how dreadful sin is.

Pay special attention to the words “for our sins.”

Our sinful nature would prefer to make itself worthy through its works before coming to Christ.

It wants the healthy person, not the person who needs a physician, to be the Savior's patient.

But Christ died not only to rescue us from God's wrath and the curse of his law.

He also came to free us from the corrupt practices and habits to which we are naturally enslaved.

Those who have not been delivered from this present evil world through the Holy Spirit's sanctifying work have no basis for assuming that Christ's blood has saved them from its condemnation.

Paul warns against another gospel (verses 6–9)

Anyone seeking a different route to heaven from the gospel of Christ is tragically deceived.

Paul rebuked the Galatians because they were abandoning justification through Christ alone.

Yet he corrected them with tenderness, recognizing that false teachers had deliberately led them astray.

When we reprove others, we must be faithful to truth while seeking to restore them gently.

Some teachers wanted to put works of the law in the place of Christ's righteousness.

By doing so, they corrupted Christianity itself.

Paul solemnly declared a curse upon anyone who tried to establish such a false foundation.

Other so-called gospels may flatter human self-righteousness or make room for worldly desires.

Either way, they are Satan's inventions rather than Christ's gospel of grace.

We must hold two truths together.

Rejecting God's moral law as a rule for Christian living dishonors Christ and destroys true religion.

But trusting our supposedly good works to justify us before God is equally fatal for anyone who persists in that false hope.

Be zealous for good deeds, but never put them where Christ's righteousness alone belongs.

And do not teach ideas that could lure others into such a dangerous deception.

Paul's message came by revelation from God (verses 10–14)

Paul's aim in preaching was to bring people into obedience to God, not to human authorities.

He would never change Christ's teaching to gain people's favor or avoid their hostility.

In matters of eternal truth, we must not fear human disapproval or seek approval through merely clever speech.

Paul received the gospel through revelation from heaven.

Unlike many Christians, he had not been led toward Christ merely by upbringing or education.

Christ's grace transformed Paul's life (verses 15–24)

God wonderfully brought Paul to the knowledge of and faith in Jesus Christ.

Everyone who is genuinely converted is called through divine grace.

Conversion is the work of God's power, acting within the heart.

It benefits us little for Christ merely to be shown to us outwardly unless he is also revealed within us.

Once Paul received this call, he prepared to obey immediately.

He did not pause to protect his wealth, public reputation, comfort or even his life.

The churches rejoiced when they heard about his conversion.

What cause for thanksgiving whenever God's people learn that a former opponent has been brought to faith!

Even believers who have never met such a person should glorify God for his power and mercy in salvation and for all the service that new believer has already rendered or may yet render to Christ's cause.
classic_reading:
[Gal.1.1-Gal.1.5]
Galatians
The churches in Galatia were formed partly of converted Jews, and partly of Gentile converts, as was generally the case. St. Paul asserts his apostolic character and the doctrines he taught, that he might confirm the Galatian churches in the faith of Christ, especially with respect to the important point of justification by faith alone. Thus the subject is mainly the same as that which is discussed in the epistle to the Romans, that is, justification by faith alone. In this epistle, however, attention is particularly directed to the point, that men are justified by faith without the works of the law of Moses. Of the importance of the doctrines prominently set forth in this epistle, Luther thus speaks: "We have to fear as the greatest and nearest danger, lest Satan take from us this doctrine of faith, and bring into the church again the doctrine of works and of men's traditions. Wherefore it is very necessary that this doctrine be kept in continual practice and public exercise, both of reading and hearing. If this doctrine be lost, then is also the doctrine of truth, life and salvation, lost and gone."
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The apostle Paul asserts his apostolic character against such as lessened it.
(1-5)
He reproves the Galatians for revolting from the gospel of Christ under the influence of evil teachers.
(6-9)
He proves the Divine authority of his doctrine and mission; and declares what he was before his conversion and calling.
(10-14)
And how he proceeded after it.
(15-24)
Verses 1-5
St. Paul was an apostle of Jesus Christ; he was expressly appointed by him, consequently by God the Father, who is one with him in respect of his Divine nature, and who appointed Christ as Mediator. Grace, includes God's good-will towards us, and his good work upon us; and peace, all that inward comfort, or outward prosperity, which is really needful for us. They come from God the Father, as the Fountain, through Jesus Christ. But observe, first grace, and then peace; there can be no true peace without grace. Christ gave himself for our sins, to make atonement for us: this the justice of God required, and to this he freely submitted. Here is to be observed the infinite greatness of the price bestowed, and then it will appear plainly, that the power of sin is so great, that it could by no means be put away except the Son of God be given for it. He that considers these things well, understands that sin is a thing the most horrible that can be expressed; which ought to move us, and make us afraid indeed. Especially mark well the words, "for our sins." For here our weak nature starts back, and would first be made worthy by her own works. It would bring him that is whole, and not him that has need of a physician. Not only to redeem us from the wrath of God, and the curse of the law; but also to recover us from wicked practices and customs, to which we are naturally enslaved. But it is in vain for those who are not delivered from this present evil world by the sanctification of the Spirit, to expect that they are freed from its condemnation by the blood of Jesus.
[Gal.1.6-Gal.1.9]
Verses 6-9
Those who would establish any other way to heaven than what the gospel of Christ reveals, will find themselves wretchedly mistaken. The apostle presses upon the Galatians a due sense of their guilt in forsaking the gospel way of justification; yet he reproves with tenderness, and represents them as drawn into it by the arts of some that troubled them. In reproving others, we should be faithful, and yet endeavour to restore them in the spirit of meekness. Some would set up the works of the law in the place of Christ's righteousness, and thus they corrupted Christianity. The apostle solemnly denounces, as accursed, every one who attempts to lay so false a foundation. All other gospels than that of the grace of Christ, whether more flattering to self-righteous pride, or more favourable to worldly lusts, are devices of Satan. And while we declare that to reject the moral law as a rule of life, tends to dishonour Christ, and destroy true religion, we must also declare, that all dependence for justification on good works, whether real or supposed, is as fatal to those who persist in it. While we are zealous for good works, let us be careful not to put them in the place of Christ's righteousness, and not to advance any thing which may betray others into so dreadful a delusion.
[Gal.1.10-Gal.1.14]
Verses 10-14
In preaching the gospel, the apostle sought to bring persons to the obedience, not of men, but of God. But Paul would not attempt to alter the doctrine of Christ, either to gain their favour, or to avoid their fury. In so important a matter we must not fear the frowns of men, nor seek their favour, by using words of men's wisdom. Concerning the manner wherein he received the gospel, he had it by revelation from Heaven. He was not led to Christianity, as many are, merely by education.
[Gal.1.15-Gal.1.24]
Verses 15-24
St. Paul was wonderfully brought to the knowledge and faith of Christ. All who are savingly converted, are called by the grace of God; their conversion is wrought by his power and grace working in them. It will but little avail us to have Christ revealed to us, if he is not also revealed in us. He instantly prepared to obey, without hesitating as to his worldly interest, credit, ease, or life itself. And what matter of thanksgiving and joy is it to the churches of Christ, when they hear of such instances to the praise of the glory of his grace, whether they have ever seen them or not! They glorify God for his power and mercy in saving such persons, and for all the service to his people and cause that is done, and may be further expected from them.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle declares his being owned as an apostle of the Gentiles.1–10He had publicly opposed Peter for judaizing.11–14And from thence he enters upon the doctrine of justification by faith in Christ, without the works of the law.15–21
The other apostles recognize Paul's calling (verses 1–10)

Paul faithfully explained the gospel he preached among the Gentiles and intended to continue preaching.

It was Christianity free from any requirement to become Jewish.

He understood that many people disliked this message, but he was not ashamed to acknowledge it.

He wanted to ensure that neither his earlier work nor his future ministry would be damaged by confusion or opposition.

Although we must trust God for the fruit of our work, we should still take reasonable precautions to prevent misunderstandings.

Some practices may be lawful in themselves.

But if accepting them in particular circumstances would betray gospel truth, we must refuse.

Nothing should be done that undermines the gospel.

Paul met the other apostles but received no addition to his knowledge or authority from them.

Recognizing the grace God had given him, they welcomed Paul and Barnabas as fellow workers.

They acknowledged Paul's equal apostolic calling, agreeing that Paul and Barnabas should go principally to the Gentiles while the others continued working among the Jews.

This division of labor agreed with Christ's purpose.

The gospel belongs to God, not to us. Ministers are entrusted with preserving and declaring it, never owning or altering it.

Paul also showed sincere charity toward Jewish believers, even though some of them were unwilling to show equal generosity toward Gentile converts.

Differences of opinion did not make him unwilling to help them.

Christians should extend such goodwill to all genuine disciples of Jesus.

Paul publicly corrects Peter's public inconsistency (verses 11–14)

Despite Peter's important calling and reputation, Paul rebuked him when his behavior harmed the truth of the gospel and the church's peace.

Peter and those who followed him acted inconsistently with the principle they professed.

Through Christ's death, the dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles had been removed, and believers were no longer bound to follow Moses' ceremonial law as a condition of acceptance.

Because Peter's error was public, Paul reproved him publicly.

Henry carefully distinguishes two actions.

Paul could wisely tolerate and temporarily observe Jewish ceremonies when they were not themselves sinful.

Peter, however, withdrew from Gentile believers in a way that encouraged people to think those ceremonies were necessary for salvation.

That was a failure of courage and a betrayal of gospel freedom.

We are justified through Christ, not the law (verses 15–19)

Having shown that he was not inferior to Peter or any other apostle, Paul turned to the gospel's foundational doctrine.

Why had they believed in Christ?

Was it not to be justified by faith in him?

Then how foolish to return to the law and expect justification by moral efforts, sacrifices or ceremonial observances!

Although the immediate controversy involved ceremonial law, the argument against dependence on moral works for justification is just as strong.

Seeking justification through Jesus does not make Christ a servant of sin.

Paul understood from the law itself that the law could not justify sinners by their works.

Its sacrifices and cleansings were no longer required because Christ had fulfilled them by offering himself for us.

As far as justification by the law was concerned, Paul was as dead to it as a dead person is to the threats of old enemies.

Yet this did not mean he could live lawlessly or carelessly.

Instead, he was freed to live for God, devoted to him through the motives and grace of the gospel.

The claim that justification by faith alone encourages sin is an old but entirely unjust accusation.

Using grace as permission for sin would make Christ the promoter of sin, a thought that should horrify every Christian heart.

Crucified with Christ, living by faith (verses 20 and 21)

Paul described the Christian's hidden spiritual life through his own experience.

The old person is crucified (Romans 6:6), yet the renewed person lives.

Sin is put to death while grace grows.

Believers enjoy the comforts and triumphs of grace, but none of that grace originates in themselves.

They live in complete dependence upon Jesus Christ.

Though still physically alive, they no longer live according to the sinful nature.

Genuine faith fixes upon Christ's personal sacrifice:

He loved me and gave himself for me.

Paul had been moving farther and farther from God.

The corruption of his desires and understanding was so great that no lesser price could have redeemed him.

Consider what Christ paid!

Some claim to believe the Christian doctrines but have only the outward form of godliness without its power.

True faith in Christ crucified means more than accepting the historical fact that he died.

It includes being crucified with him, leaving the old way of life behind.

Grace can never be combined with human merit as its basis.

It would cease to be grace if it were not entirely free.

The more fully we depend on Christ for everything, the more willingly we obey his commandments.

He lives and rules within the believer.

We live by faith in the Son of God—a faith that works through love, produces obedience and transforms us toward his holy likeness.

Such a believer neither misuses God's grace nor treats it as worthless.
classic_reading:
[Gal.2.1-Gal.2.10]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The apostle declares his being owned as an apostle of the Gentiles. | (1-10) |
He had publicly opposed Peter for judaizing. | (11-14) |
And from thence he enters upon the doctrine of justification by faith in Christ, without the works of the law. | (15-21) |
Verses 1-10
Observe the apostle's faithfulness in giving a full account of the doctrine he had preached among the Gentiles, and was still resolved to preach, that of Christianity, free from all mixture of Judaism. This doctrine would be ungrateful to many, yet he was not afraid to own it. His care was, lest the success of his past labours should be lessened, or his future usefulness be hindered. While we simply depend upon God for success to our labours, we should use every proper caution to remove mistakes, and against opposers. There are things which may lawfully be complied with, yet, when they cannot be done without betraying the truth, they ought to be refused. We must not give place to any conduct, whereby the truth of the gospel would be reflected upon. Though Paul conversed with the other apostles, yet he did not receive any addition to his knowledge, or authority, from them. Perceiving the grace given to him, they gave unto him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, whereby they acknowledged that he was designed to the honour and office of an apostle as well as themselves. They agreed that these two should go to the heathen, while they continued to preach to the Jews; judging it agreeable to the mind of Christ, so to divide their work. Here we learn that the gospel is not ours, but God's; and that men are but the keepers of it; for this we are to praise God. The apostle showed his charitable disposition, and how ready he was to own the Jewish converts as brethren, though many would scarcely allow the like favour to the converted Gentiles; but mere difference of opinion was no reason to him why he should not help them. Herein is a pattern of Christian charity, which we should extend to all the disciples of Christ.
[Gal.2.11-Gal.2.14]
Verses 11-14
Notwithstanding Peter's character, yet, when Paul saw him acting so as to hurt the truth of the gospel and the peace of the church, he was not afraid to reprove him. When he saw that Peter and the others did not live up to that principle which the gospel taught, and which they professed, namely, That by the death of Christ the partition wall between Jew and Gentile was taken down, and the observance of the law of Moses was no longer in force; as Peter's offence was public, he publicly reproved him. There is a very great difference between the prudence of St. Paul, who bore with, and used for a time, the ceremonies of the law as not sinful, and the timid conduct of St. Peter, who, by withdrawing from the Gentiles, led others to think that these ceremonies were necessary.
[Gal.2.15-Gal.2.19]
Verses 15-19
Paul, having thus shown he was not inferior to any apostle, not to Peter himself, speaks of the great foundation doctrine of the gospel. For what did we believe in Christ? Was it not that we might be justified by the faith of Christ? If so, is it not foolish to go back to the law, and to expect to be justified by the merit of moral works, or sacrifices, or ceremonies? The occasion of this declaration doubtless arose from the ceremonial law; but the argument is quite as strong against all dependence upon the works of the moral law, as respects justification. To give the greater weight to this, it is added, But if, while we seek to be justified by Christ, we ourselves also are found sinners, is Christ the minister of sin? This would be very dishonourable to Christ, and also very hurtful to them. By considering the law itself, he saw that justification was not to be expected by the works of it, and that there was now no further need of the sacrifices and cleansings of it, since they were done away in Christ, by his offering up himself a sacrifice for us. He did not hope or fear any thing from it; any more than a dead man from enemies. But the effect was not a careless, lawless life. It was necessary, that he might live to God, and be devoted to him through the motives and grace of the gospel. It is no new prejudice, though a most unjust one, that the doctrine of justification by faith alone, tends to encourage people in sin. Not so, for to take occasion from free grace, or the doctrine of it, to live in sin, is to try to make Christ the minister of sin, at any thought of which all Christian hearts would shudder.
[Gal.2.20-Gal.2.21]
Verses 20-21
Here, in his own person, the apostle describes the spiritual or hidden life of a believer. The old man is crucified, [Rom.6.6] Ro 6:6, but the new man is living; sin is mortified, and grace is quickened. He has the comforts and the triumphs of grace; yet that grace is not from himself, but from another. Believers see themselves living in a state of dependence on Christ. Hence it is, that though he lives in the flesh, yet he does not live after the flesh. Those who have true faith, live by that faith; and faith fastens upon Christ's giving himself for us. He loved me, and gave himself for me. As if the apostle said, The Lord saw me fleeing from him more and more. Such wickedness, error, and ignorance were in my will and understanding, that it was not possible for me to be ransomed by any other means than by such a price. Consider well this price. Here notice the false faith of many. And their profession is accordingly; they have the form of godliness without the power of it. They think they believe the articles of faith aright, but they are deceived. For to believe in Christ crucified, is not only to believe that he was crucified, but also to believe that I am crucified with him. And this is to know Christ crucified. Hence we learn what is the nature of grace. God's grace cannot stand with man's merit. Grace is no grace unless it is freely given every way. The more simply the believer relies on Christ for every thing, the more devotedly does he walk before Him in all his ordinances and commandments. Christ lives and reigns in him, and he lives here on earth by faith in the Son of God, which works by love, causes obedience, and changes into his holy image. Thus he neither abuses the grace of God, nor makes it in vain.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Galatians reproved for departing from the great doctrine of justification alone, through faith in Christ.1–5This doctrine established from the example of Abraham.6–9From the tenor of the law and the severity of its curse.10–14From the covenant of promises, which the law could not disannul.15–18The law was a school master to lead them to Christ.19–25Under the gospel state true believers are all one in Christ.26–29
Christ crucified and the Spirit received by faith (verses 1–5)

The Galatians' departure from the gospel was especially unreasonable because Christ crucified had already been clearly preached among them.

They had also participated in the Lord's Supper, where his suffering and its meaning had been set before them.

Had they received the Holy Spirit by keeping the Mosaic law or by any meritorious works of their own?

No.

They received him by hearing and believing the message of justification through faith in Christ alone.

God's favor and approval had been demonstrated through that message.

How foolish to reject the ministry and doctrine through which God had already blessed them!

Sadly, people often turn from Christ crucified, the very heart of Christianity, toward empty distinctions, moral instruction without the Savior or unsupported religious speculations.

Satan works through different people and methods to blind minds so they will not trust the crucified Redeemer.

Where are the Spirit's fruits most clearly produced—where salvation is taught by works of law, or where it is taught by faith in Christ?

Henry answers confidently: among those who proclaim justification by faith.

Abraham was accepted by faith; Christ bore the curse (verses 6–14)

Paul used Abraham's example to prove the gospel doctrine the Galatians had abandoned.

Abraham trusted God's word and promise.

Through that faith he was regarded by God as righteous.

When Scripture is said to foresee something, the Holy Spirit who inspired it is the One who foresaw.

Abraham was blessed by believing God's promise, and others receive that blessing in the same way.

Let us study what Abraham trusted, the nature of his faith and the effects it produced.

No one escapes the law's curse through obedience, because its curse falls upon sinners and all have sinned.

A lawbreaker already stands under condemnation and cannot look to the same law as a way of earning acquittal.

The righteous are those rescued from death and wrath and brought into life under God's favor.

This happens through faith, not meritorious works.

Justification by faith was not an invention of the Christian era.

It was taught long before Christ's coming and has always been the only way sinners have been justified.

Though the law cannot free us from its own curse, faith in Christ can.

Jesus redeemed us by being made a curse for us.

Henry explains that Christ was made sin as a sin offering, not himself made sinful, and was placed for a time under divine punishment—not separated from God.

His suffering warns sinners to flee God's righteous wrath more strongly than the law's threats alone.

If the Father did not spare his Son when he bore our sins, how can the unrepentant expect to escape judgment?

Yet from the cross Christ freely invites sinners to take refuge in him.

God's covenant promise was not cancelled by the law (verses 15–18)

The covenant God made with Abraham was not cancelled when the law came through Moses.

God's promise was given to Abraham and his Seed.

It continues through Christ, who lives forever, and through those who belong to him by faith.

This helps us understand the difference between the law's promises and the gospel's promises.

The law addresses each individual person under its requirements.

The gospel's promises are made first to Christ, and then through him to those who are joined to Christ by faith.

We must distinguish promise and law, not only as abstract teachings but also in how they shape our desires and our lives.

If the promise is made dependent upon legal merit, it is turned back into law.

Keep Christ continually before your eyes as the sure defense of faith against any attempt to rely upon human righteousness.

The law reveals sin and points toward the promise (verses 19–22)

If God's promise already provided salvation, why was the law added?

Even Israel, the people chosen for special privileges, remained sinful.

The law did not introduce a second route to justification.

Instead, it revealed the seriousness of sin and showed sinners their need for God's promise.

It pointed toward Jesus Christ, through whom alone sins could be forgiven and people made righteous.

The promise came directly from God.

The law was given through the ministry of angels and through a mediator, Moses.

It could not therefore have been intended to cancel the earlier promise.

A mediator acts between parties, not merely for one against the other.

The law's great purpose was that, recognizing their guilt and inability to achieve righteousness by lawkeeping, sinners might believe in Christ and receive the promised blessing through faith.

God's holy, just and good law, which remains the standard of moral duty, cannot be an enemy of Christ's gospel.

When correctly understood, it supports the gospel's purpose.

The law leads sinners to Christ as a teacher leads a child (verses 23–25)

The ceremonial law could not itself give saving knowledge and life.

Its practices, especially sacrifices, pointed forward to Christ so that sinners might be justified through faith.

In this sense the law was like a servant charged with taking a child to school.

It led people to Christ, the Teacher who reveals the true way of justification and salvation.

The gospel gives believers a much clearer knowledge of divine grace and mercy than the older order did.

Many people remain like prisoners in a dark dungeon, content in their sins and blinded by Satan through worldly pleasures and interests.

When the sinner awakens, the true danger becomes clear.

God's grace and mercy now appear as the only hope.

The Holy Spirit often uses the law's warnings to awaken a conscience and reveal the need for Christ.

The sinner is moved to rely upon Christ's suffering and merits for justification by faith.

Then the law, under the Spirit's instruction, becomes a loved rule of duty and a standard for daily self-examination.

Used in this way, it leads the believer to depend more completely, not less completely, upon the Savior.

Through faith, believers become God's children in Christ (verses 26–29)

Genuine Christians enjoy privileges far greater than those experienced under the old covenant.

They are no longer treated like distant servants but received as children of God.

Having accepted Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior and relying upon him for justification and salvation, they receive the status of sons and daughters.

But no outward form or profession, by itself, secures these privileges.

Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not truly belong to him.

In baptism, believers put on Christ and openly profess themselves his disciples.

Baptism points toward being joined with Christ's death and resurrection, so that believers die to sin and live in newness and holiness.

But putting on Christ according to the gospel is not merely outward imitation.

It requires new birth and complete inward change.

The God who makes believers heirs will provide for them.

Therefore let us carry out the duties entrusted to us and commit every other care into his hands.

Our greatest concern should be heaven.

This world's things are small by comparison.

The heavenly city of God is the inheritance of his children.

Above all, seek to be assured of that inheritance.
classic_reading:
[Gal.3.1-Gal.3.5]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The Galatians reproved for departing from the great doctrine of justification alone, through faith in Christ. | (1-5) |
This doctrine established from the example of Abraham. | (6-9) |
From the tenor of the law and the severity of its curse. | (10-14) |
From the covenant of promises, which the law could not disannul. | (15-18) |
The law was a school master to lead them to Christ. | (19-25) |
Under the gospel state true believers are all one in Christ. | (26-29) |
Verses 1-5
Several things made the folly of the Galatian Christians worse. They had the doctrine of the cross preached, and the Lord's supper administered among them, in both which Christ crucified, and the nature of his sufferings, had been fully and clearly set forth. Had they been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, by the ministration of the law, or on account of any works done by them in obedience thereto? Was it not by their hearing and embracing the doctrine of faith in Christ alone for justification? Which of these had God owned with tokens of his favour and acceptance? It was not by the first, but the last. And those must be very unwise, who suffer themselves to be turned away from the ministry and doctrine which have been blessed to their spiritual advantage. Alas, that men should turn from the all-important doctrine of Christ crucified, to listen to useless distinctions, mere moral preaching, or wild fancies! The god of this world, by various men and means, has blinded men's eyes, lest they should learn to trust in a crucified Saviour. We may boldly demand where the fruits of the Holy Spirit are most evidently brought forth? whether among those who preach justification by the works of the law, or those who preach the doctrine of faith? Assuredly among the latter.
[Gal.3.6-Gal.3.14]
Verses 6-14
The apostle proves the doctrine he had blamed the Galatians for rejecting; namely, that of justification by faith without the works of the law. This he does from the example of Abraham, whose faith fastened upon the word and promise of God, and upon his believing he was owned and accepted of God as a righteous man. The Scripture is said to foresee, because the Holy Spirit that indited the Scripture did foresee. Through faith in the promise of God he was blessed; and it is only in the same way that others obtain this privilege. Let us then study the object, nature, and effects of Abraham's faith; for who can in any other way escape the curse of the holy law? The curse is against all sinners, therefore against all men; for all have sinned, and are become guilty before God: and if, as transgressors of the law, we are under its curse, it must be vain to look for justification by it. Those only are just or righteous who are freed from death and wrath, and restored into a state of life in the favour of God; and it is only through faith that persons become righteous. Thus we see that justification by faith is no new doctrine, but was taught in the church of God, long before the times of the gospel. It is, in truth, the only way wherein any sinners ever were, or can be justified. Though deliverance is not to be expected from the law, there is a way open to escape the curse, and regain the favour of God, namely, through faith in Christ. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law; being made sin, or a sin-offering, for us, he was made a curse for us; not separated from God, but laid for a time under the Divine punishment. The heavy sufferings of the Son of God, more loudly warn sinners to flee from the wrath to come, than all the curses of the law; for how can God spare any man who remains under sin, seeing that he spared not his own Son, when our sins were charged upon him? Yet at the same time, Christ, as from the cross, freely invites sinners to take refuge in him.
[Gal.3.15-Gal.3.18]
Verses 15-18
The covenant God made with Abraham, was not done away by the giving the law to Moses. The covenant was made with Abraham and his Seed. It is still in force; Christ abideth for ever in his person, and his spiritual seed, who are his by faith. By this we learn the difference between the promises of the law and those of the gospel. The promises of the law are made to the person of every man; the promises of the gospel are first made to Christ, then by him to those who are by faith ingrafted into Christ. Rightly to divide the word of truth, a great difference must be put between the promise and the law, as to the inward affections, and the whole practice of life. When the promise is mingled with the law, it is made nothing but the law. Let Christ be always before our eyes, as a sure argument for the defence of faith, against dependence on human righteousness.
[Gal.3.19-Gal.3.22]
Verses 19-22
If that promise was enough for salvation, wherefore then serveth the law? The Israelites, though chosen to be God's peculiar people, were sinners as well as others. The law was not intended to discover a way of justification, different from that made known by the promise, but to lead men to see their need of the promise, by showing the sinfulness of sin, and to point to Christ, through whom alone they could be pardoned and justified. The promise was given by God himself; the law was given by the ministry of angels, and the hand of a mediator, even Moses. Hence the law could not be designed to set aside the promise. A mediator, as the very term signifies, is a friend that comes between two parties, and is not to act merely with and for one of them. The great design of the law was, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ, might be given to those that believe; that, being convinced of their guilt, and the insufficiency of the law to effect a righteousness for them, they might be persuaded to believe on Christ, and so obtain the benefit of the promise. And it is not possible that the holy, just, and good law of God, the standard of duty to all, should be contrary to the gospel of Christ. It tends every way to promote it.
[Gal.3.23-Gal.3.25]
Verses 23-25
The law did not teach a living, saving knowledge; but, by its rites and ceremonies, especially by its sacrifices, it pointed to Christ, that they might be justified by faith. And thus it was, as the word properly signifies, a servant, to lead to Christ, as children are led to school by servants who have the care of them, that they might be more fully taught by Him the true way of justification and salvation, which is only by faith in Christ. And the vastly greater advantage of the gospel state is shown, under which we enjoy a clearer discovery of Divine grace and mercy than the Jews of old. Most men continue shut up as in a dark dungeon, in love with their sins, being blinded and lulled asleep by Satan, through wordly pleasures, interests, and pursuits. But the awakened sinner discovers his dreadful condition. Then he feels that the mercy and grace of God form his only hope. And the terrors of the law are often used by the convincing Spirit, to show the sinner his need of Christ, to bring him to rely on his sufferings and merits, that he may be justified by faith. Then the law, by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, becomes his loved rule of duty, and his standard for daily self-examination. In this use of it he learns to depend more simply on the Saviour.
[Gal.3.26-Gal.3.29]
Verses 26-29
Real Christians enjoy great privileges under the gospel; and are no longer accounted servants, but sons; not now kept at such a distance, and under such restraints as the Jews were. Having accepted Christ Jesus as their Lord and Saviour, and relying on him alone for justification and salvation, they become the sons of God. But no outward forms or profession can secure these blessings; for if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his. In baptism we put on Christ; therein we profess to be his disciples. Being baptized into Christ, we are baptized into his death, that as he died and rose again, so we should die unto sin, and walk in newness and holiness of life. The putting on of Christ according to the gospel, consists not in outward imitation, but in a new birth, an entire change. He who makes believers to be heirs, will provide for them. Therefore our care must be to do the duties that belong to us, and all other cares we must cast upon God. And our special care must be for heaven; the things of this life are but trifles. The city of God in heaven, is the portion or child's part. Seek to be sure of that above all things.

From bondage to the adoption of God's children (verses 1–7)

Paul spoke plainly against those trying to combine the Mosaic law with the gospel in a way that brought believers back into bondage.

The old covenant contained many demanding ceremonies and restrictions.

Like a child placed under tutors and guardians, God's people lived under a form of instruction that did not yet reveal fully what those observances meant.

The gospel brings Christians into a happier and freer condition.

These verses display the wonder of God's love.

The Father sent his Son into the world for our redemption.

The Son humbled himself and suffered for us.

The Holy Spirit graciously comes to dwell in believers' hearts.

We were by nature children of disobedience and exposed to divine wrath.

Through grace we become children whom God loves, and the Spirit begins shaping us into the family likeness.

In human families only the eldest son commonly received the special inheritance.

But every one of God's children shares the inheritance of an eldest son.

May our attitudes and actions demonstrate our adoption!

May the Holy Spirit bear witness with our spirits that we are God's children and heirs.

Do not return to the slavery of false worship (verses 8–11)

The Gentile Christians had turned from idols to the living God and had received adoption through Christ.

This change came entirely through God's free and generous grace.

How serious, then, to abandon the freedom he had given!

All genuine knowledge of God begins with him.

We know him because he first knew us.

Although Christianity forbids worshiping idols, many still practice idolatry in their hearts.

Whatever a person loves and values most becomes that person's god.

Some make wealth their god; others enthrone pleasure or sinful desire.

Some worship an imaginary god who possesses only mercy and no justice.

They assume God will pardon them even as they refuse repentance and continue in sin.

Even people who once professed faith confidently can be drawn away from the simplicity and purity of the gospel.

The more mercy God has shown us in giving us gospel knowledge and freedom, the greater our foolishness if we surrender those blessings.

Members of the visible church should therefore examine themselves carefully rather than resting in a few outward signs of religious life.

Paul feared that his labor might have accomplished little, yet he continued laboring.

Perseverance in duty despite uncertain results is wisdom and reverence toward God.

Each person should follow this rule in the place and calling assigned to them.

Paul appeals to the Galatians as their friend (verses 12–18)

Paul wanted the Galatians to agree with him about the Mosaic law, but also to remain united with him in love.

Whenever we correct someone, we should make clear that the correction comes from concern for God's honor and that person's genuine welfare.

Paul reminded them of the physical difficulty he had experienced when he first preached among them.

At that time they had welcomed him gladly as God's messenger.

But human admiration and respect are sadly unstable.

We should labor above all to be approved by God.

The Galatians once regarded themselves as happy to receive Christ's gospel.

Why should they now act as though it had been a mistake?

Christians must not stop telling the truth merely because some people might feel offended by it.

The false teachers pretended affection for the Galatians, but their motives were self-serving rather than sincere.

Paul gave an excellent rule: be zealous in a good cause at all times.

Zeal should not appear briefly and then vanish. It should remain steady.

How blessed the church would be if believers held to that kind of faithful eagerness!

Paul's concern until Christ is formed in them (verses 19 and 20)

The Galatians had begun to regard Paul almost as an enemy.

Yet he assured them of his genuine friendship and parental affection.

He was deeply troubled about their spiritual condition and wanted to learn whether they would recover from their present deception.

The strongest evidence that a sinner has received justification is that Christ is being formed within that person through the renewing work of the Holy Spirit.

But this inward transformation cannot be expected while someone continues seeking acceptance with God through the law instead of Christ.

Hagar and Sarah picture two covenant arrangements (verses 21–27)

Paul illustrated the difference between relying upon Christ and relying upon the law through Isaac and Ishmael.

The historical account of Sarah and Hagar has its ordinary literal meaning, but Paul explained that the Holy Spirit also intended it to point toward a deeper spiritual truth.

The two women form suitable pictures of two different covenant arrangements.

Sarah represents the heavenly Jerusalem, God's true church, living in freedom and becoming the spiritual mother of believers.

Those born of the Holy Spirit and united to Christ through genuine faith belong to Abraham's promised spiritual descendants.

Paul applied this interpretation to his readers.

Believers are children of the free woman, not the slave woman.

Since their privileges under the gospel are so great, it would be absurd for Gentile Christians to return to a legal arrangement that could not rescue even unbelieving Jews from spiritual bondage or condemnation.

Henry makes an important qualification.

We would not have identified this allegorical meaning in Sarah and Hagar if the apostle had not revealed it, but because the Holy Spirit disclosed it through Paul, its divine intention is certain.

The allegory explains the teaching rather than serving as an independent proof of it.

It illustrates the covenant of works and covenant of grace, and the attitudes of legalistic and gospel-minded religion.

Good works attempted in a person's own strength belong to the legalistic spirit.

Works arising from faith in Christ reflect the gospel.

The first spirit produces bondage to sin and death.

The second produces freedom—not freedom to sin, but freedom to fulfill duty.

The first spirit leads to persecution, while the second is marked by love.

People who treat God's servants with a violent, harsh or controlling spirit should examine themselves.

Even a genuine believer may temporarily fall back into an approach based upon personal merit or self-strength, especially through unbelief or neglect of God's promises.

Such a person may also treat other believers harshly instead of lovingly.

Yet this is not the believer's settled way of life.

A genuine believer will find no rest until returning to dependence on Christ.

Let us ground our hope upon Scripture and demonstrate through cheerful obedience that our hearts and treasure truly belong in heaven.
classic_reading:
[Gal.4.1-Gal.4.7]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The folly of returning to legal observances for justification. | (1-7) |
The happy change made in the Gentile believers. | (8-11) |
The apostle reasons against following false teachers. | (12-18) |
He expresses his earnest concern for them. | (19-20) |
And then explains the difference between what is to be expected from the law, and from the gospel. | (21-31) |
Verses 1-7
The apostle deals plainly with those who urged the law of Moses together with the gospel of Christ, and endeavoured to bring believers under its bondage. They could not fully understand the meaning of the law as given by Moses. And as that was a dispensation of darkness, so of bondage; they were tied to many burdensome rites and observances, by which they were taught and kept subject like a child under tutors and governors. We learn the happier state of Christians under the gospel dispensation. From these verses see the wonders of Divine love and mercy; particularly of God the Father, in sending his Son into the world to redeem and save us; of the Son of God, in submitting so low, and suffering so much for us; and of the Holy Spirit, in condescending to dwell in the hearts of believers, for such gracious purposes. Also, the advantages Christians enjoy under the gospel. Although by nature children of wrath and disobedience, they become by grace children of love, and partake of the nature of the children of God; for he will have all his children resemble him. Among men the eldest son is heir; but all God's children shall have the inheritance of eldest sons. May the temper and conduct of sons ever show our adoption; and may the Holy Spirit witness with our spirits that we are children and heirs of God.
[Gal.4.8-Gal.4.11]
Verses 8-11
The happy change whereby the Galatians were turned from idols to the living God, and through Christ had received the adoption of sons, was the effect of his free and rich grace; they were laid under the greater obligation to keep to the liberty wherewith he had made them free. All our knowledge of God begins on his part; we know him because we are known of him. Though our religion forbids idolatry, yet many practise spiritual idolatry in their hearts. For what a man loves most, and cares most for, that is his god: some have their riches for their god, some their pleasures, and some their lusts. And many ignorantly worship a god of their own making; a god made all of mercy and no justice. For they persuade themselves that there is mercy for them with God, though they repent not, but go on in their sins. It is possible for those who have made great professions of religion, to be afterwards drawn aside from purity and simplicity. And the more mercy God has shown, in bringing any to know the gospel, and the liberties and privileges of it, the greater their sin and folly in suffering themselves to be deprived of them. Hence all who are members of the outward church should learn to fear and to suspect themselves. We must not be content because we have some good things in ourselves. Paul fears lest his labour is in vain, yet he still labours; and thus to do, whatever follows, is true wisdom and the fear of God. This every man must remember in his place and calling.
[Gal.4.12-Gal.4.18]
Verses 12-18
The apostle desires that they would be of one mind with him respecting the law of Moses, as well as united with him in love. In reproving others, we should take care to convince them that our reproofs are from sincere regard to the honour of God and religion and their welfare. The apostle reminds the Galatians of the difficulty under which he laboured when he first came among them. But he notices, that he was a welcome messenger to them. Yet how very uncertain are the favour and respect of men! Let us labour to be accepted of God. You once thought yourselves happy in receiving the gospel; have you now reason to think otherwise? Christians must not forbear speaking the truth, for fear of offending others. The false teachers who drew the Galatians from the truth of the gospel were designing men. They pretended affection, but they were not sincere and upright. An excellent rule is given. It is good to be zealous always in a good thing; not for a time only, or now and then, but always. Happy would it be for the church of Christ, if this zeal was better maintained.
[Gal.4.19-Gal.4.20]
Verses 19-20
The Galatians were ready to account the apostle their enemy, but he assures them he was their friend; he had the feelings of a parent toward them. He was in doubt as to their state, and was anxious to know the result of their present delusions. Nothing is so sure a proof that a sinner has passed into a state of justification, as Christ being formed in him by the renewal of the Holy Spirit; but this cannot be hoped for, while men depend on the law for acceptance with God.
[Gal.4.21-Gal.4.27]
Verses 21-27
The difference between believers who rested in Christ only, and those who trusted in the law, is explained by the histories of Isaac and Ishmael. These things are an allegory, wherein, beside the literal and historical sense of the words, the Spirit of God points out something further. Hagar and Sarah were apt emblems of the two different dispensations of the covenant. The heavenly Jerusalem, the true church from above, represented by Sarah, is in a state of freedom, and is the mother of all believers, who are born of the Holy Spirit. They were by regeneration and true faith, made a part of the true seed of Abraham, according to the promise made to him.
[Gal.4.28-Gal.4.31]
Verses 28-31
The history thus explained is applied. So then, brethren, we are not children of the bond-woman, but of the free. If the privileges of all believers were so great, according to the new covenant, how absurd for the Gentile converts to be under that law, which could not deliver the unbelieving Jews from bondage or condemnation! We should not have found out this allegory in the history of Sarah and Hagar, if it had not been shown to us, yet we cannot doubt it was intended by the Holy Spirit. It is an explanation of the subject, not an argument in proof of it. The two covenants of works and grace, and legal and evangelical professors, are shadowed forth. Works and fruits brought forth in a man's own strength, are legal. But if arising from faith in Christ, they are evangelical. The first covenant spirit is of bondage unto sin and death. The second covenant spirit is of liberty and freedom; not liberty to sin, but in and unto duty. The first is a spirit of persecution; the second is a spirit of love. Let those professors look to it, who have a violent, harsh, imposing spirit, towards the people of God. Yet as Abraham turned aside to Hagar, so it is possible a believer may turn aside in some things to the covenant of works, when through unbelief and neglect of the promise he acts according to the law, in his own strength; or in a way of violence, not of love, towards the brethren. Yet it is not his way, not his spirit to do so; hence he is never at rest, till he returns to his dependence on Christ again. Let us rest our souls on the Scriptures, and by a gospel hope and cheerful obedience, show that our conversation and treasure are indeed in heaven.

Stand firm in the freedom Christ gives (verses 1–6)

Christ will not be the Savior of anyone who refuses to trust and receive him as the only Savior.

We must heed Paul's warning to remain firm in the doctrine and freedom of the gospel.

The Holy Spirit teaches true believers to await everlasting life and righteousness as God's gift through faith in Christ, not as payment for their own good works.

A Jewish Christian might continue observing certain traditional ceremonies or make use of the freedom not to observe them.

A Gentile believer might likewise disregard those customs or participate in them.

The decisive issue was not trusting those practices as the basis of acceptance with God.

No outward privilege or religious label can make a person acceptable without genuine faith in Jesus Christ.

True faith is active: it works through love for God and for fellow believers.

May we be among those who, through the Spirit, await the hope of righteousness by faith.

The danger does not lie in the indifferent character of some outward ceremonies.

It lies in attaching saving value to them in place of faith in Christ.

Without faith expressing itself in love, everything else is worthless by comparison.

Keep running the Christian race without accepting false teaching (verses 7–12)

Christian life is like a race.

We must run faithfully and continue until the prize is obtained.

Simply claiming the name Christian is not enough.

Our manner of life should agree with that profession.

Many begin well but become distracted, slow down or leave the path.

Those who notice their faith weakening should ask seriously: What is hindering me?

The false teaching troubling the Galatians added works of the law to faith in Christ as necessary for justification.

Paul showed that such persuasion did not come from God but from Satan.

Churches must beware of encouraging those who follow destructive error and especially those who spread it.

When correcting wrongdoing, we should distinguish teachers who mislead from people who have been misled.

Some Jewish opponents resented the gospel's claim that Christ alone saves sinners.

If Paul had agreed that Mosaic observances must be added to faith for salvation, he and other believers might have avoided much persecution.

But even the first traces of this corrupting leaven had to be resisted.

People who persist in disturbing Christ's church with such teaching will face God's judgment.

Gospel freedom is for loving service, not sin (verses 13–15)

The gospel teaches godliness (1 Timothy 6:3).

It never provides permission to indulge sin.

On the contrary, Christ's freedom gives us the strongest reasons to resist and put sin to death.

The whole moral law is summarized in the command to love your neighbor as yourself.

Believers should help and encourage one another.

If they instead attack one another because of different opinions, the resulting conflict opens the way for spiritual harm.

The God of love may withdraw the felt comfort of his grace; the Spirit of love is resisted, and the evil spirit who seeks destruction gains an advantage.

How much better if Christians spent less energy biting and devouring one another and more energy opposing sin within themselves and their communities!

Walk by the Spirit and cultivate his fruit (verses 16–26)

When believers seek to live under the guidance and power of the Holy Spirit, sinful desires may still arise and struggle against them.

But those desires need not rule over them.

The Christian life involves a real conflict between remaining corruption and renewing grace.

Genuine believers long for the Spirit's grace to gain a complete and speedy victory.

Those who yield themselves to the Holy Spirit are no longer under the law as a covenant requiring merit or exposed to its curse.

Their hatred of sin and desire for holiness show the reality of the salvation they have received.

The works of the flesh are numerous and plainly sinful.

People who persist in them will not inherit heaven.

How terrible that many who profess Christianity nevertheless continue those practices while claiming to expect salvation!

The fruit of the Spirit describes the qualities produced by a renewed heart.

As Paul's list of sinful practices particularly includes actions that injure people and relationships, his list of spiritual fruits especially emphasizes attitudes and actions that make Christians kind and beneficial toward one another.

The Spirit's fruit both benefits the believer and makes Christian fellowship more joyful.

These traits give evidence of the Spirit's guidance.

The contrast teaches us which practices we must resist and which virtues we must cultivate.

Genuine Christians take that duty seriously.

Sin must no longer reign in their mortal bodies (Romans 6:12).

They seek to put it to death, not merely excuse it.

Christ will not acknowledge as his faithful people those who voluntarily surrender themselves as slaves to sin.

And it is not enough merely to stop doing wrong: we must learn to do good.

Our conduct follows the power that governs our hearts (Romans 8:5).

Let us labor to put the body's sinful deeds to death and to live in spiritual newness.

Do not seek vain praise, provoke one another or become envious.

Instead, cultivate more abundantly the good fruits which through Jesus Christ bring praise and glory to God.

[Gal.5.1-Gal.5.6]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
An earnest exhortation to stand fast in the liberty of the gospel. | (1-12) |
To take heed of indulging a sinful temper. | (13-15) |
And to walk in the Spirit, and not to fulfil the lusts of the flesh: the works of both are described.
(16-26)
Verses 1-6
Christ will not be the Saviour of any who will not own and rely upon him as their only Saviour. Let us take heed to the warnings and persuasions of the apostle to stedfastness in the doctrine and liberty of the gospel. All true Christians, being taught by the Holy Spirit, wait for eternal life, the reward of righteousness, and the object of their hope, as the gift of God by faith in Christ; and not for the sake of their own works. The Jewish convert might observe the ceremonies or assert his liberty, the Gentile might disregard them or might attend to them, provided he did not depend upon them. No outward privileges or profession will avail to acceptance with God, without sincere faith in our Lord Jesus. True faith is a working grace; it works by love to God, and to our brethren. May we be of the number of those who, through the Spirit, wait for the hope of righteousness by faith. The danger of old was not in things of no consequence in themselves, as many forms and observances now are. But without faith working by love, all else is worthless, and compared with it other things are of small value.
[Gal.5.7-Gal.5.12]
Verses 7-12
The life of a Christian is a race, wherein he must run, and hold on, if he would obtain the prize. It is not enough that we profess Christianity, but we must run well, by living up to that profession. Many who set out fairly in religion, are hindered in their progress, or turn out of the way. It concerns those who begin to turn out of the way, or to tire in it, seriously to inquire what hinders them. The opinion or persuasion, ver. #(8), was, no doubt, that of mixing the works of the law with faith in Christ in justification. The apostle leaves them to judge whence it must arise, but sufficiently shows that it could be owing to none but Satan. It is dangerous for Christian churches to encourage those who follow, but especially who spread, destructive errors. And in reproving sin and error, we should always distinguish between the leaders and the led. The Jews were offended, because Christ was preached as the only salvation for sinners. If Paul and others would have admitted that the observance of the law of Moses was to be joined with faith in Christ, as necessary to salvation, then believers might have avoided many of the sufferings they underwent. The first beginnings of such leaven should be opposed. And assuredly those who persist in disturbing the church of Christ must bear their judgment.
[Gal.5.13-Gal.5.15]
Verses 13-15
The gospel is a doctrine according to godliness, [1Tim.6.3] 1Ti 6:3, and is so far from giving the least countenance to sin, that it lays us under the strongest obligation to avoid and subdue it. The apostle urges that all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. If Christians, who should help one another, and rejoice one another, quarrel, what can be expected but that the God of love should deny his grace, that the Spirit of love should depart, and the evil spirit, who seeks their destruction, should prevail? Happy would it be, if Christians, instead of biting and devouring one another on account of different opinions, would set themselves against sin in themselves, and in the places where they live.
[Gal.5.16-Gal.5.26]
Verses 16-26
If it be our care to act under the guidance and power of the blessed Spirit, though we may not be freed from the stirrings and oppositions of the corrupt nature which remains in us, it shall not have dominion over us. Believers are engaged in a conflict, in which they earnestly desire that grace may obtain full and speedy victory. And those who desire thus to give themselves up to be led by the Holy Spirit, are not under the law as a covenant of works, nor exposed to its awful curse. Their hatred of sin, and desires after holiness, show that they have a part in the salvation of the gospel. The works of the flesh are many and manifest. And these sins will shut men out of heaven. Yet what numbers, calling themselves Christians, live in these, and say they hope for heaven! The fruits of the Spirit, or of the renewed nature, which we are to do, are named. And as the apostle had chiefly named works of the flesh, not only hurtful to men themselves, but tending to make them so to one another, so here he chiefly notices the fruits of the Spirit, which tend to make Christians agreeable one to another, as well as to make them happy. The fruits of the Spirit plainly show, that such are led by the Spirit. By describing the works of the flesh and fruits of the Spirit, we are told what to avoid and oppose, and what we are to cherish and cultivate; and this is the sincere care and endeavour of all real Christians. Sin does not now reign in their mortal bodies, so that they obey it, [Rom.6.12] Ro 6:12, for they seek to destroy it. Christ never will own those who yield themselves up to be the servants of sin. And it is not enough that we cease to do evil, but we must learn to do well. Our conversation will always be answerable to the principle which guides and governs us, [Rom.8.5] Ro 8:5. We must set ourselves in earnest to mortify the deeds of the body, and to walk in newness of life. Not being desirous of vain-glory, or unduly wishing for the esteem and applause of men, not provoking or envying one another, but seeking to bring forth more abundantly those good fruits, which are, through Jesus Christ, to the praise and glory of God.

Carry one another's burdens (verses 1–5)

Christians should carry one another's burdens.

Doing this fulfills the law of Christ, which calls us to mutual patience, compassion and practical support.

We travel through life together and should help fellow travelers under heavy loads.

It is easy to assume that we are wiser and better than others and therefore entitled to lecture them.

But that attitude is self-deception.

Someone who claims a superiority that does not exist will eventually discover the bitter consequences.

Such pride wins no genuine respect from God or other people.

Paul calls every believer to examine their own work.

The better we know our hearts and conduct, the less likely we are to despise others—and the more willing we become to help them through weakness and suffering.

Sins that seem small when committed become a heavy burden when their account must be given before God.

No one can pay another person's ransom through personal ability.

Sin is a spiritual weight upon the soul.

When someone feels no weight of guilt at all, that is reason for especially serious self-examination.

Many people are spiritually dead and therefore have no awareness of sin's burden.

When we recognize its weight, we should seek release through the Savior and learn to avoid every sin.

Sow to the Spirit and do good without growing weary (verses 6–11)

Some people neglect religious duties while continuing to display an outward profession.

They may deceive other people, but they cannot deceive God.

He knows both conduct and motive, and he will not be mocked.

This present life is sowing time.

In the world to come, we shall reap the result of what is sown now.

There are two kinds of sowing: to the flesh and to the Spirit.

Those who live under the rule of sinful desires should expect misery and ruin, not eternal happiness.

But those who, under the Holy Spirit's guidance, live by faith in Christ and cultivate the graces of Christian living will reap everlasting life from the Spirit.

We often become tired of doing our duty, particularly doing good for others.

We must guard against that discouragement.

The promised reward is given to those who persevere in good work.

Every person should seek opportunities for useful service within their own responsibilities and means.

Do good while you are alive, making it a central purpose of your life.

When new opportunities arise, act on them as far as your abilities allow.

Boast only in Christ's cross and become a new creation (verses 12–15)

Proud and worldly-minded people often want just enough religion to preserve an impressive public appearance.

Paul's greatest source of joy and honor, however, was the cross of Jesus Christ.

By the cross he meant Christ's suffering and death, the saving work of the crucified Redeemer.

Through Christ's cross, the world is crucified to the believer and the believer to the world.

The more we contemplate what the Savior endured from this world, the less attractive its praise and pleasures become.

Henry illustrates this with the dreadful appearance of someone dying by crucifixion.

The person beholding such suffering is not charmed by the victim's former physical beauty.

Nor would a dying person hanging upon a cross be captivated by the earthly scenes still visible in the final moments.

Likewise, to those who truly believe in Jesus Christ, worldly attractions lose their power in comparison with him.

There is a new creation.

Old attitudes and desires give way to a new understanding and way of living through the regenerating work of the Holy Spirit.

Believers enter a new world.

Created in Christ for good works, they receive a life increasingly marked by holiness.

This change affects the mind and heart, leading us to trust Jesus and live for God.

Where such genuine inward and practical faith is missing, outward religious labels and professions accomplish nothing.

Peace and mercy in the grace of Christ (verses 16–18)

The greatest distinction between people is not status or religious ceremony, but a new creation formed in Christ's likeness through faith.

God promises peace and mercy to those who walk according to this rule.

Peace includes reconciliation with God, an untroubled conscience and the earthly comforts genuinely needed for our good.

Mercy means a share in the free love and favor of God in Christ, the fountain from which every other blessing flows.

God's written word must guide us, in both doctrine and conduct.

May his grace always be with our spirits, sanctifying, enlivening and comforting us.

May we remain ready to defend the honor of the truth that gives us life.

Paul carried the marks of Jesus in his own body—scars received from persecutors because he remained faithful to Christ and the gospel.

He addressed the Galatians as brothers and sisters, displaying humility and tender love.

He ended by praying that they would receive Christ's gracious favor, both in its actual benefits and in the assurance that it was theirs.

We need no greater blessing for happiness than the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul prayed not that Moses' law or righteousness earned by works would remain with them, but that Christ's grace would live in their hearts and spirits, giving life, comfort and strength.

His final Amen expressed both his earnest wish that this blessing might be theirs and his confidence that it would be granted.
classic_reading:
[Gal.6.1-Gal.6.5]
Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
Exhortations to meekness, gentleness, and humility. | (1-5) |
To kindness towards all men, especially believers. | (6-11) |
The Galatians guarded against the judaizing teachers. | (12-15) |
A solemn blessing. | (16-18) |
Verses 1-5
We are to bear one another's burdens. So we shall fulfil the law of Christ. This obliges to mutual forbearance and compassion towards each other, agreeably to his example. It becomes us to bear one another's burdens, as fellow-travellers. It is very common for a man to look upon himself as wiser and better than other men, and as fit to dictate to them. Such a one deceives himself; by pretending to what he has not, he puts a cheat upon himself, and sooner or later will find the sad effects. This will never gain esteem, either with God or men. Every one is advised to prove his own work. The better we know our own hearts and ways, the less shall we despise others, and the more be disposed to help them under infirmities and afflictions. How light soever men's sins seem to them when committed, yet they will be found a heavy burden, when they come to reckon with God about them. No man can pay a ransom for his brother; and sin is a burden to the soul. It is a spiritual burden; and the less a man feels it to be such, the more cause has he to suspect himself. Most men are dead in their sins, and therefore have no sight or sense of the spiritual burden of sin. Feeling the weight and burden of our sins, we must seek to be eased thereof by the Saviour, and be warned against every sin.
[Gal.6.6-Gal.6.11]
Verses 6-11
Many excuse themselves from the work of religion, though they may make a show, and profess it. They may impose upon others, yet they deceive themselves if they think to impose upon God, who knows their hearts as well as actions; and as he cannot be deceived, so he will not be mocked. Our present time is seed time; in the other world we shall reap as we sow now. As there are two sorts of sowing, one to the flesh, and the other to the Spirit, so will the reckoning be hereafter. Those who live a carnal, sensual life, must expect no other fruit from such a course than misery and ruin. But those who, under the guidance and influences of the Holy Spirit, live a life of faith in Christ, and abound in Christian graces, shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting. We are all very apt to tire in duty, particularly in doing good. This we should carefully watch and guard against. Only to perseverance in well-doing is the reward promised. Here is an exhortation to all to do good in their places. We should take care to do good in our life-time, and make this the business of our lives. Especially when fresh occasions offer, and as far as our power reaches.
[Gal.6.12-Gal.6.15]
Verses 12-15
Proud, vain, and carnal hearts, are content with just so much religion as will help to keep up a fair show. But the apostle professes his own faith, hope, and joy; and that his principal glory was in the cross of Christ. By which is here meant, his sufferings and death on the cross, the doctrine of salvation by a crucified Redeemer. By Christ, or by the cross of Christ, the world is crucified to the believer, and he to the world. The more we consider the sufferings of the Redeemer from the world, the less likely shall we be to love the world. The apostle was as little affected by its charms, as a beholder would be by any thing which had been graceful in the face of a crucified person, when he beholds it blackened in the agonies of death. He was no more affected by the objects around him, than one who is expiring would be struck with any of the prospects his dying eyes might view from the cross on which he hung. And as to those who have truly believed in Christ Jesus, all things are counted as utterly worthless compared with him. There is a new creation; old things are passed away, and new views and dispositions are brought in under the regenerating influences of God the Holy Spirit. Believers are brought into a new world, and being created in Christ Jesus unto good works, are formed to a life of holiness. It is a change of mind and heart, whereby we are enabled to believe in the Lord Jesus, and to live to God; and where this inward, practical religion is wanting, outward professions, or names, will never stand in any stead.
[Gal.6.16-Gal.6.18]
Verses 16-18
A new creation to the image of Christ, as showing faith in him, is the greatest distinction between one man and another, and a blessing is declared on all who walk according to this rule. The blessings are, peace and mercy. Peace with God and our conscience, and all the comforts of this life, as far as they are needful. And mercy, an interest in the free love and favour of God in Christ, the spring and fountain of all other blessings. The written word of God is the rule we are to go by, both in its doctrines and precepts. May his grace ever be with our spirit, to sanctify, quicken, and cheer us, and may we always be ready to maintain the honour of that which is indeed our life. The apostle had in his body the marks of the Lord Jesus, the scars of wounds from persecuting enemies, for his cleaving to Christ, and the doctrine of the gospel. The apostle calls the Galatians his brethren, therein he shows his humility and his tender affection for them; and he takes his leave with a very serious prayer, that they might enjoy the favour of Christ Jesus, both in its effects and in its evidences. We need desire no more to make us happy than the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. The apostle does not pray that the law of Moses, or the righteousness of works, but that the grace of Christ, might be with them; that it might be in their hearts and with their spirits, quickening, comforting, and strengthening them: to all which he sets his Amen; signifying his desire that so it might be, and his faith that so it would be.
